title: The demons at dawn
hook: demons attack the sun at every twilight and the prayers' water drives them back; why Hindus pray at the junctions of the day

segments.voice: Yesterday, morning puja, and Kubja's sandal paste. Your line was puja is serving God with your own hands. A new week starts today, the week of sunset and arti, and it opens with a question: when?
screen: `MORNING PUJA — PUJA IS SERVING GOD WITH YOUR OWN HANDS.`

segments.voice: Here's an old story about every sunrise you've ever seen. At the edges of the day, a horde of demons called the Mandehas rise up and rush at the sun, trying to swallow it. They're under a curse: they die each day and come back each night, so the fight never ends. Every dawn, every dusk, they attack again. And what drives them back? Not armies. Not the other gods. People at prayer, standing at a riverbank, throwing a little water toward the sun. In the telling, that water, made holy by the prayer, strikes the demons like thunderbolts. And the sun climbs.
screen: `DEMONS RUSH AT THE SUN.` → `EVERY DAWN, EVERY DUSK.` → `PEOPLE AT THE RIVER, THROWING WATER.` → `THE SUN CLIMBS.`

segments.voice: That's how the Vishnu Purana tells it, and the same story is in older Vedic texts. Notice when the fight happens: not at midday, not at midnight. At the edges. Today's word is sandhya. It comes from a word for joining, the place where two things meet. So sandhya means twilight, and more: the joints of the day. Tradition names three. Dawn, where night meets day. Noon, where morning turns. Dusk, where day meets night. These are the hours Hindus set aside for prayer. The old rite for them is sandhyavandana, honoring the junctions, and at its heart is the Gayatri, the prayer to the light from day one hundred eight, said while offering water to the sun. That's the arghya from the story. It's traditionally kept by those who wear the sacred thread; many other Hindus keep a simpler form: water poured toward the morning sun, or the evening lamp lit at dusk while the house pauses. Why the edges? Many teachers say a junction belongs to neither side, so it's a door in the ordinary, and a door can be guarded. They read the demons as the darkness that tries to slip in when one part of the day hands over to the next. That's the teaching: Hindus tie prayer to the turning of the day itself, and they stand at the door when it turns.
screen: `SANDHYA — A JOINING.` · `DAWN, NOON, DUSK.` · `SANDHYAVANDANA: THE GAYATRI AND WATER TO THE SUN.` · `A JUNCTION IS A DOOR.`

segments.voice: If it's near dawn or dusk, find a window or step outside; if it isn't, remember the last sunrise or sunset you really watched. Look at the light and notice it changing. If you pray, this is one of the hours tradition sets aside: pour a little water toward the light, or just lift your hands, and say the Gayatri if you know it, or a name you honor, once. If you don't pray, simply stand at the edge of the day and notice it turn.
Sandhya. A joining: the twilight, and the three junctions of the day, dawn, noon and dusk, when the prayers go up and the sun climbs.
Your line: pray where the day joins. That's where the old story says the light needs you. One hundred eighteen days in.

screen: `PRAY WHERE THE DAY JOINS.` → `DAY 118 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: NARADA'S MONKEY FACE.`

what a scholar hears: sandhyā is from sam-dhā, to put together; the Mandeha story (Taittiriya Aranyaka 2.2; Vishnu Purana 2.8) explains the arghya of sandhyāvandana, the thrice-daily rite with the Gayatri at its center, traditionally enjoined on those who wear the sacred thread.
